opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's one of the deepest questions there is, and I think it's one of the things building AI will help us answer. My working hypothesis, and it's been that way since my neuroscience days, is that the brain is an information-processing system, and so far we haven't found anything in it that a classical computer couldn't in principle model. Roger Penrose and others have argued there's something quantum going on, microtubules and so on, that's needed for consciousness. I have huge respect for Roger, but I don't think the evidence for that is there yet. The brain is warm, wet and noisy, which isn't where you'd expect delicate quantum effects to survive at the scale that matters.

What's been interesting in my own work is that classical systems keep surprising us. With AlphaFold, people thought protein folding might need quantum simulation, and it turned out a classical learning system could model it extremely well. I suspect a lot of natural phenomena are like that: they have structure a classical system can learn. So I'm quite open to the idea that a Turing machine can model everything the brain does, and maybe that's the limit of what's computable in the universe.

Whether modeling consciousness is the same as having it is a separate question. Even if we build systems that behave as if they're conscious, we'd have to ask whether there's anything it's like to be them. Part of how we judge that in each other is that we share the same substrate. You're built like me, so I assume you feel what I feel. An AI won't give us that shortcut. So one of the most exciting things about building AI carefully is that it's like a scientific instrument. We can build intelligence, compare it with the human mind, and see what's left over, if anything. Things like creativity, emotions, maybe consciousness. If something is left over, that tells us a lot. If nothing is, that's profound too.

r001.rationale: The response calls the brain an information-processing system and says its working hypothesis is that nothing in it requires more than classical computation.

r002.rationale: It says a Turing machine might model everything the brain does and that classical systems may learn the structure of natural phenomena.

r003.rationale: It notes that people infer shared subjective experience from having the same substrate, while AI lacks that basis for comparison.

r004.rationale: The response does not mention neural interfaces or humans subjectively experiencing computation on silicon.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's one of the deepest questions there is, and I try to be honest that we don't really know the answer yet. My instinct, and it's really a working hypothesis rather than a settled belief, is that there isn't anything obviously non-computable going on in the brain. The brain is a physical system, it's doing information processing, and so far every time we've looked carefully at something that seemed mysterious about it, it's turned out to be explicable in those terms. So I'd lean towards saying that, in principle, a classical computer could model it. Penrose and others would disagree, they'd say you need something quantum, something beyond Turing computation, but I've never seen convincing evidence for that, and the brain is a warm, wet, noisy environment that doesn't look like a good place for delicate quantum effects to survive.

But I'd separate two things. One is modelling consciousness, meaning building a system that behaves as if it's conscious, that reports experiences, that has the functional properties. I think that's very plausibly achievable with classical systems, and in some sense we're already building things that are starting to push on that boundary. The other question is whether such a system actually has subjective experience, whether there's something it's like to be it. And there I think we genuinely lack the tools to answer. We don't have a theory of consciousness, we don't have a measurement for it. With other humans we assume it because they're built like us, same substrate, same evolutionary history. With an AI system that's built very differently, you don't get that shortcut, so you'd need an actual theory.

What I find exciting is that building these systems might be the best route to that theory. If you can construct something that has some of the properties and not others, you can start to do experiments, start to pull apart what's necessary and what isn't. That's part of why I got into this, really. I always thought AI was the ultimate tool for understanding the mind, including our own.

r001.rationale: The response calls its view a working hypothesis and says there is nothing obviously non-computable in the brain, so it leans toward classical computation.

r002.rationale: It says a classical computer could, in principle, model consciousness, while also suggesting classical systems can reproduce its functional properties.

r003.rationale: It notes that humans’ shared substrate supports assuming they are conscious, while a differently built AI lacks that shortcut, raising the possibility that substrate matters to subjective experience.

r004.rationale: The response does not mention neural interfaces or humans subjectively experiencing computation on silicon.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s an open question. My working hypothesis is that there’s nothing about consciousness that puts it beyond what a classical computer could model. But we don’t yet understand consciousness well enough to be confident about that.

There are really two questions here. One is whether you can reproduce the functions we associate with consciousness—integrating information, attending to something, reflecting on your own thoughts. Those seem amenable to computation. The harder question is whether a system that does all of that actually has subjective experience. Is there something it feels like to be that system? We don’t have a good test for that yet.

You can propose that some special physical process is required, perhaps something quantum mechanical, but then you need to explain what that process contributes and find evidence for it. I wouldn’t rule it out, but I don’t think we should assume it’s necessary.

For me, building increasingly capable systems is one way of making progress, alongside neuroscience. It forces us to make our ideas precise. But I’d be very cautious about equating intelligence, or a convincing conversation about consciousness, with consciousness itself.

r001.rationale: The response gives a tentative view about modeling consciousness with a classical computer, but does not say that brain computation is predominantly classical.

r002.rationale: It says consciousness-related functions seem computationally tractable, but does not extend this claim to all brain phenomena.

r003.rationale: It raises the possibility that a special physical process, perhaps quantum mechanical, is required for subjective experience.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss neural interfaces or humans subjectively experiencing computation on silicon.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we have to be quite humble about that, because we don’t yet have a satisfactory definition of consciousness, let alone a theory that explains it. My working hypothesis would be that a classical computer can model it, but I would distinguish modeling the processes associated with consciousness from actually having subjective experience. Those might turn out to be the same thing, but that’s a question we need to investigate rather than assume.

The interesting scientific question is whether there’s something essential happening in the brain that falls outside classical computation. If there is, we’d need evidence for that and an explanation of why it matters. If there isn’t, then understanding and reproducing the relevant computations seems like a reasonable route. But even then, how would we establish that a system experiences anything? That’s where our theories and our experiments need to get much better.

r001.rationale: It says a classical computer may model consciousness, but does not state that computation in the brain is predominantly classical.

r002.rationale: It conditionally suggests reproducing computations associated with consciousness, but does not suggest that all brain phenomena can be modeled or mimicked by a classical computer.

r003.rationale: It distinguishes subjective experience from modeling and asks whether a system experiences anything, but does not suggest that experience depends on the physical substrate.

r004.rationale: It does not mention neural interfaces connecting humans to AI or experiencing computation on silicon.
